newsitem.title: THAILAND: Banker backs Thai central bank's baht defence.
newsitem.headline: Banker backs Thai central bank's baht defence.

text.p: The Bank of Thailand on Monday got a major morale boost in its battle against currency speculators who have stepped up attacks on the baht in the past several weeks.
Olarn Chaipravat, president of the Thai Bankers Association, told a press conference he saw no logic for Thailand to devalue the baht, a move he said would fail to help exports.

The banker, current chief executive of the Siam Commercial Bank Plc, voiced his full support for a central bank policy to curb speculation against the baht by reducing money supply through high domestic interest rates.
"Under Thailand's current export structure and globalised trade, a devaluation would not only fail to help exports, it will also bring national bankruptcy," he said.
Olarn said Thai central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond would issue a major statement on Tuesday to reiterate that he has no plan to devalue the baht.

The banker, who turned down offers of many past governments to take over the finance portfolio, said he does not expect the central bank to hesitate using all its resources, including Thailand's $38.7 billion foreign reserves, to defend its currency.

"For the central bank, it's a do-or-die battle. But for hedge fund managers, it's just a money game. They are like a pack of vultures circling over a victim. Once they realise that the bank means business in fighting back, they will just quit and move on to other targets," he said.
Olarn said he expects hedge fund managers would put up an ante of a few billion dollars to test the will of the Thai central bank.
The baht has declined to its 6-1/2 year low against a surging U.S. dollar in the past month while it appreciated against the yen and mark.
The baht is fixed daily against a basket of major currencies in which, traders estimate, the U.S. dollar accounts for about 82 percent, the yen 12 percent, and mark six percent.
Olarn said a baht devaluation will not necessarily make Thai exports cheaper as most of them carry an average 43 percent of import content which would cost more after the currency is devalued.

The banker said about 35 percent of imports last year were intermediate raw materials, oil and other goods used by the export sector while another 53 percent were capital goods including machinery and vehicles.

He said a devaluation would inflate the cost of these imports, further eroding export competitiveness. "Devaluation will not help our trade balance which, in Thailand's case, should be rectified by deepening our industrial restructuring," he said.
Olarn said with Thailand's current total outstanding foreign debt of about $90 billion, a 10 percent baht devaluation would add at least $nine billion of national debt.
